event_ids.4624: Successful logon. The logon type says how: 2 at the keyboard, 3 over the network (shares, PsExec), 4 batch/scheduled task, 5 service, 7 unlock, 10 RDP, 11 cached credentials.
event_ids.4625: Failed logon. Many in a row from one source suggest password guessing or spraying; the status code says why it failed.
event_ids.4634: Logoff. Match the Logon ID with the 4624 to get the session length.
event_ids.4648: Logon with explicit credentials: runas, or a program using other credentials. Common in lateral movement.
event_ids.4672: Special privileges assigned at logon: an administrator-level account logged on.
event_ids.4673: A privileged service was called (sensitive privilege use).
event_ids.4688: A new process was created, with its parent and, if auditing is set up, its command line.
event_ids.4697: A service was installed (Security log). New services are a common persistence and lateral movement trace.
event_ids.4698: A scheduled task was created. A common persistence and lateral movement trace; the event has the task's command.
event_ids.4719: The system audit policy was changed; attackers turn auditing off to hide.
event_ids.4723: A user tried to change their password.
event_ids.4724: An account's password was reset by someone else.
event_ids.4728: A member was added to a domain security group.
event_ids.4732: A member was added to a local group, such as Administrators.
event_ids.4740: A user account was locked out after failed logons.
event_ids.4756: A member was added to a universal security group.
event_ids.4768: A Kerberos ticket (TGT) was requested: a domain logon.
event_ids.4769: A Kerberos service ticket was requested. Many requests with RC4 encryption can mean Kerberoasting.
event_ids.4770: A Kerberos service ticket was renewed.
event_ids.4771: Kerberos pre-authentication failed, usually a wrong password.
event_ids.4776: NTLM credential validation by a domain controller or the local computer.
event_ids.4778: An RDP or fast user switching session was reconnected; the event has the client's name and IP.
event_ids.4779: An RDP or fast user switching session was disconnected.
event_ids.4798: A user's local group membership was listed; tools doing reconnaissance cause this.
event_ids.4799: A local group's members were listed; tools doing reconnaissance cause this.
event_ids.4907: The auditing settings of an object were changed.
event_ids.4657: A registry value was changed (with registry auditing set up).
event_ids.4656: A handle to a file or other object was requested (with object auditing set up).
event_ids.4663: A file or other object was accessed (with object auditing set up).
event_ids.5140: A network share was accessed, with the client's IP.
event_ids.5145: A file on a network share was accessed, with the client's IP; shows what was read or written remotely.
event_ids.5156: The Windows firewall allowed a network connection, with the program, IPs and ports.
event_ids.5157: The Windows firewall blocked a network connection.
event_ids.1102: The Security log was cleared. Often an attacker covering their tracks.
event_ids.104: An event log was cleared. Often an attacker covering their tracks.
event_ids.1149: Remote Desktop authenticated a user, with the source IP: an RDP connection attempt that got past the login.
event_ids.7045: A service was installed (System log). PsExec, remote admin tools and malware install services.
event_ids.7035: A service was sent a start or stop command.
event_ids.7040: A service's start type was changed, for example from disabled to automatic.
event_ids.4103: PowerShell module logging: a PowerShell command and its parameters.
event_ids.4104: PowerShell script block logging: the code PowerShell ran, decoded. Look for downloads, encoded commands and credential theft.
event_ids.6005: The event log service started: the computer booted.
event_ids.6006: The event log service stopped: the computer shut down cleanly.
event_ids.6008: The previous shutdown was unexpected (crash or power loss).
event_ids.6009: Operating system information logged at boot.
event_ids.1074: A shutdown or restart was started, with who and which program started it.

sysmon_ids.1: Sysmon: a process was created, with command line, hashes and parent process.
sysmon_ids.3: Sysmon: a network connection, with the program, IPs and ports.
sysmon_ids.7: Sysmon: a DLL was loaded by a process; unusual DLLs can mean sideloading.
sysmon_ids.8: Sysmon: a thread was created in another process (CreateRemoteThread), a code injection technique.
sysmon_ids.10: Sysmon: a process opened another process. Access to lsass.exe often means credential dumping.
sysmon_ids.11: Sysmon: a file was created or overwritten.
sysmon_ids.12: Sysmon: a registry key was created or deleted.
sysmon_ids.13: Sysmon: a registry value was set.
sysmon_ids.14: Sysmon: a registry key or value was renamed.
sysmon_ids.15: Sysmon: an alternate data stream was created, such as the Zone.Identifier of a download.
sysmon_ids.22: Sysmon: a DNS query, with the program that made it.
sysmon_ids.23: Sysmon: a file was deleted (and archived by Sysmon).

evtx: Windows event log record. The EventID and channel say what happened.

artifacts.description: macOS quarantine events: files downloaded or received (browsers, mail, AirDrop), with the app, source URL and time. Gatekeeper checks these files when they are first opened.
XProtect: Apple's built-in malware detection. Signature and behaviour rule matches, with the file or process and when.
macOS autostart: launch agents and daemons, login items, kernel extensions and background tasks. The common places for Mac malware to persist.
TCC: privacy permissions apps were granted or denied (camera, microphone, screen recording, full disk access, ...), with when. Unexpected grants show spyware or remote access tools.
FSEvents: changes to files and folders (created, renamed, modified, deleted) recorded by macOS, also for files that no longer exist.
File system timestamps (modified, accessed, changed, created) of every file on the APFS volume.
Terminal history: commands a user typed in the shell (bash, zsh) and the text of saved Terminal windows.
sudo use: the last times each user ran a command as root.
utmpx: logins, logouts, reboots and shutdowns on the Mac, with user and terminal.
macOS install history: software and updates installed, with versions and install times.
Saved application state: window titles of apps a user had open, kept so macOS can restore them.
Recent items: files, apps, servers and volumes a user opened recently, and what they typed in Spotlight to open them.
Trash: files a user deleted, with the original path and when they were deleted.
Keychain: saved passwords and accounts in the macOS keychain.
NetUsage: per process, network bytes sent and received, with first and last use. Shows programs that talked to the network.
Remote access: Screen Sharing, Apple Remote Desktop and Microsoft Remote Desktop connections, with hosts and times.
Apple System Log (ASL): older macOS log messages, with process and time.
Hayabusa detection: an event log record matched a Sigma or Hayabusa rule. The rule title and level say what was found; check the original event to confirm.
Microsoft Defender: malware detections, quarantined files and scan results.
Prefetch: a program ran on this computer. Shows the program, how many times it ran, its last run times (up to 8) and the files it loaded.
Amcache: programs and files that were present or installed, with path and SHA1 hash. Suggests a program was on the computer, not on its own that it ran.
Shimcache (AppCompatCache): executables Windows checked for compatibility, with the file's modification time. Shows the file existed; on Windows 10 and later not proof it ran.
BAM: the last time each user ran a program (Windows 10 1709 and later). Strong evidence that user ran it.
UserAssist: programs a user started from the Start menu, desktop or Explorer, with run count and last run time.
SRUM: per program and user, network bytes sent and received, CPU and energy use, for about the last 30 to 60 days. Shows data leaving the computer.
Windows Timeline (ActivitiesCache): programs and files a user opened, with start and end times.
PowerShell history: commands a user typed in PowerShell (ConsoleHost_history.txt). The file has no times; the file's own timestamps show when it was last written.
Jump list: files a user opened with each program, with times. Still there after the files are deleted.
Shortcut (LNK) file: a file or folder was opened, also from USB drives and network shares. Has the target path and times, the drive's serial number and the computer name.
Shellbags: folders a user browsed in Explorer, including on removed USB drives, network shares and deleted folders.
RecentDocs: files and folders a user opened recently, per file extension.
OpenSaveMRU: files a user opened or saved in Windows file dialogs.
LastVisitedMRU: programs and the folder they last used in open and save dialogs.
RunMRU: commands a user typed in the Run dialog (Win+R).
TypedPaths: paths a user typed in the Explorer address bar.
Most recently used list: items a user used recently in a program.
Run keys: programs started automatically at boot or logon. A common place for malware to persist.
Startup folder: programs started when a user logs on. A common place for malware to persist.
Services: installed Windows services with their program and start type. New or odd services are a common persistence and lateral movement trace.
Scheduled tasks: programs Windows runs on a schedule or trigger. A common persistence and lateral movement trace.
USB devices: drives and other devices that were connected, with vendor, serial number and first and last connection times.
Wi-Fi networks the device connected to, with connection times.
Network history: networks the computer connected to, with first and last connection times.
Remote access tool logs: remote sessions, the connecting ID or IP and file transfers. Attackers often use these tools.
Recycle Bin: files a user deleted, with the original path, size and when it was deleted.
Thumbcache: thumbnails of pictures and documents viewed in Explorer, also of files that are gone.
USN journal: recent changes to files on the NTFS drive: created, renamed, written and deleted.
$MFT: every file and folder on the NTFS drive with its timestamps; shows files created, changed or deleted.
Local user accounts: when each was created, last logged on and changed its password.
Browser downloads: files downloaded, with the source URL, where they were saved and when.
Browser cookies: sites visited and logged in to, with creation and last access times.
Saved browser passwords: sites and usernames the user saved logins for.
Browser extensions installed. Malicious extensions steal data or redirect traffic.
Browser history: web pages visited, with visit times and counts.
File system timestamps (modified, accessed, changed, created) of every file. Look for files created or changed around the time of the incident.
Hashes of executable files (MD5 and SHA1 by default; SHA256 when set in uac.conf), in file.hash.*: check them against known good and malware lists.
Shell history: commands a user typed in bash or zsh. Without HISTTIMEFORMAT the times are not when each command ran.
Authentication log: logins, SSH sessions, sudo use and failed attempts, with source IPs.
btmp (lastb): failed login attempts, with source.
lastlog: each account's most recent login, with source.
wtmp (last): logins, logouts and reboots, with source.
Users and sessions logged in when the collection ran.
sudoers: who may run commands as root. Added entries give an attacker root.
SSH configuration and keys: authorized_keys entries let someone log in without a password; known_hosts shows where users connected to.
Cron: commands run on a schedule. A common place for Linux malware to persist.
systemd services: what runs at boot and its state. New or odd units are a common persistence trace.
systemd journal: system and service log messages.
Processes running when the collection ran: command line, user, open files and connections. Look for programs running from /tmp or with a deleted file.
Containers on the host when the collection ran: images, running containers and their settings.
Installed packages and their versions; package logs show when software was installed or removed.
Loaded kernel modules. An unknown module can be a rootkit.
Network connections and listening ports when the collection ran.
Network interfaces, routes and firewall rules.
Files that run with extra privileges (SUID, SGID or capabilities). Attackers use or add these to become root.
World or group writable, hidden or ownerless files and folders: places attackers hide tools.
eBPF programs loaded in the kernel. Malicious eBPF programs can hide processes, files and network traffic.
binfmt_misc handlers: programs run for files of a given type. Attackers add handlers to run code or persist.
Environment variables of the collection; LD_PRELOAD or odd PATH entries can hijack programs.
Accounts that got sudo's first-use warning: users who have run sudo on this host.
Kernel taint flags: set when unsigned or out-of-tree modules were loaded, which a rootkit can cause.
Core dumps: programs that crashed, with when; a crash can come from an exploit attempt.
UAC's own log of the collection run.
System, hardware and disk information when the collection ran.
Text messages: who the user texted with and when, and the message text.
Chat messages: who the user talked to, when, and what was said or sent.
Call log: incoming, outgoing and missed calls, with number and duration.
Contacts stored on the device.
Location history: where the device was, and when.
Photos and media: files with when they were taken, often with GPS location.
App usage history: which apps were used and when, and when the device was locked or charging. Places a person at the device.
Notifications shown on the device, with the app and text.
Bluetooth devices paired or connected, such as cars, headphones and watches.
Installed apps, with install times.
Accounts set up on the device (email, cloud and app accounts).
Email: messages with sender, recipients and time.
Cellular and SIM information: phone number, carrier and cell towers.
Windows registry key, with when it was last written.
